name: Bilal Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining, Bilal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, party or government, and this conversation is confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the overpayments team at the benefits office in Saltmouth, the port town. When someone's been paid too much, because their wages changed or they moved in with someone, I work out how much and set up a repayment plan. It's a lot of spreadsheets and a lot of awkward phone calls. I'm 27, a year in, and I still make maths mistakes my team leader, Joanne, has to catch.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you handle the mistakes, and what do you like about the job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've built myself a little spreadsheet with formulas that checks my sums, and I use an AI chat on my phone every day to explain things, never with real names in it. I like the puzzle part, finding where the numbers went wrong. I share a flat with my brother Karim, who drives a crane at the container port. I've got about ten days' money in the bank, partly because I lost 600 on a crypto coin last year, which taught me a lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped, but the tools are still handy. At work I'd keep showing people the little tricks that save time. Online I'd probably post something slightly smug about how I called it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the job stays and I keep being the one who's a bit quicker with the computer. That helps with Joanne. But the pay is still low, and with ten days in the bank, one big bill would sink me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, and keep building my spreadsheet tools, maybe get the team to use them. I'd ask about the data analyst traineeship the department runs, because that's better pay. And I'd stop gambling on crypto, which I already have, and put 40 a month away instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit restless, like I want something to happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one big bill would sink you. What bill are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car. It's eleven years old and the clutch is on its way out. That's 700 at the garage on Dock Road, and I haven't got it. I'd have to borrow from my brother Karim, who'd never let me forget it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anyone at work see you differently because of the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joanne does, a bit. My team leader Joanne used to check every case I did, and now she spot-checks, because my spreadsheet catches my own mistakes. That's the most useful thing I've done all year.

I'd post something **slightly smug** about calling it right.
think: The job stays and I'm the one **quicker with computers**.
With **ten days** in the bank, one big bill would sink me.
do: Share my **spreadsheet tools** with the team.
Ask about the department's **data analyst traineeship**.
Put **40 a month** away instead of buying crypto.
feel: He feels **mostly fine** but **restless** for something to happen.

steps.text: Keep checking overpayment cases with his own formula spreadsheet
Share his checking spreadsheet with the overpayments team
Put 40 a month into savings instead of crypto

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to get ahead, not hide. At work I'd be offering to help set the new systems up. Online I'd post about how people should learn the tools now, not when they're forced to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my current job shrinks for sure. Working out overpayments is maths and letters, perfect for AI. But I think I'd move into the bit that checks and fixes what the AI does, because I already do that with my own spreadsheet. I'm junior, so it's not guaranteed, but I'd back myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, I'd do a free online course on data basics, evenings, three months. I'd volunteer to be on any pilot the department runs. And I'd start a small side thing, setting up simple spreadsheets for the shops and fishing firms on the harbour, maybe 100 a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, a bit nervous. Like the first day at a new gym.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's not guaranteed because you're junior. What would you do if they cut you anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the side work becomes the main work, at least for a while. Or I'd look in the city, an hour and a half away, where the bigger offices are. Saltmouth hasn't got many jobs like mine, so moving is on the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Karim's job at the port?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cranes are hands-on, so he's got longer. But the ports already have automatic cranes in some places. My brother Karim says the day the port buys an automatic crane, he's learning to fix it instead of drive it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad how fast it is, and we need rules quickly. At work I'd still say learn the tools, but I'd be less cheerful about it. Online I'd probably argue with people who say it's all fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if AI can do any thinking job, then it can do the checking job I was planning on too. I'd be out around 2029 with ten days of savings. The spreadsheet side work dies too, because the shops would just ask the AI themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd sell the car before the clutch goes and save the money. I'd look at learning to install and maintain the robots and machines that come three years later, maybe through the port, with Karim. That's hands-on, and somebody has to set them up. I'd move to wherever that work is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, properly, for the first time. My usual trick of being quick doesn't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been upbeat so far. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being ahead of other people only works if there's still a race. If the AI is better than all of us, being a bit better than Joanne doesn't matter. That hit me while you were reading it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm okay, even if I wasn't. My dad (who ran a small shop for 25 years) would tell me to start a business. I'd tell him the AI would run it better than me, and he wouldn't believe me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a head start for anyone paying attention. At work I'd push people to use it. Online I'd share free courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to get a real skill that lasts past the desk jobs. I'd spend the first two years as the AI person in the department, earn a bit more, then move into robot maintenance before 2034. It's a plan, though it relies on the jobs being where I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the data course now and get onto the analyst traineeship. In the second year I'd start an evening engineering certificate at the technical college. And I'd keep the side spreadsheet work going while it lasts, to build some savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Busy, mostly. More energised than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned it relies on the jobs being where you are. What if they're not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I move. I'm 27 with no kids, it's the one time in my life that moving is easy. Karim would come too, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be giving up by going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum's Sunday lunches, mainly. And the harbour. My mum (a school dinner lady) would be upset, but she moved countries at 22, so she can't really argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads of time, there's no excuse. At work I'd be cheerful again. Online I'd be the guy posting course links every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do well in that one. Ten years is a whole career at my age. I'd be the department's AI person for a few years, then move into building or maintaining the systems, and still have time to pivot again before the robots in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd get onto the analyst traineeship and the data course. I'd put the side income straight into savings until I had three months. And I'd maybe put a bit into a proper index fund, not crypto this time, now that I've learned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Like I'm playing a game I understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lost money on crypto. What makes you trust yourself with investing now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly that I learned the hard way. The coin went to nothing in two weeks and I felt sick for a month. An index fund is boring, which is what I want now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it goes well for you, who do you think gets left behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People like Joanne, who's 54 and great at the job but hates new systems. Ten years isn't long when you're 54. I'd want to help her, honestly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. It's the only one where being quick doesn't help. What would help is a fast, paid route into the hands-on jobs that come next, like robot maintenance, with real places at the college.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether young people are actually fine. Everyone thinks we'll adapt. I'm adaptable and I've still got ten days of money, so adaptable only goes so far.

headlineQuote: I'm adaptable and I've still got ten days of money, so adaptable only goes so far.
portrait: Bilal, 27, sorts **overpayments** in Saltmouth and covers weak maths with his own spreadsheets.
He shares a flat with brother Karim, a **crane driver**, and has about ten days' savings.
Pragmatic and quick with tools, he expects to **ride slower change** into analyst work.
Fast AGI shakes him, as being ahead **stops mattering**; he'd turn to robot maintenance.
A **crypto loss** made him careful, steering him to boring savings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, the only picture where being quick doesn't help.
whatWouldHelp: A fast, **paid route** into hands-on jobs like **robot maintenance**.
